one_liner: Rust research serialization library and kernel-bypass UDP stack that sends large fields zero-copy via NIC scatter-gather, beating Protobuf/FlatBuffers/Cap'n Proto.
what_it_does: Cornflakes compiles proto3 schemas into Rust objects (plus C bindings with opaque void* handles) that have Protobuf-style getters, setters, list init/append and deserialize functions. The library is co-designed with its own kernel-bypass UDP stack (custom Mellanox OFED and Intel ICE datapaths, partial DPDK). You do not call serialize into a byte buffer: you pass the object to the connection (send_object / serialize_and_send), and the stack builds the packet. It is not a drop-in replacement: I/O data must come from the stack's pinned, reference-counted buffers, and the wire format resembles Cap'n Proto/FlatBuffers, so it is not Protobuf-wire-compatible.
how_it_is_fast: Protobuf, FlatBuffers and Cap'n Proto copy each bytes/string field into a contiguous buffer and then again into DMA memory; Cornflakes instead posts each pinned-memory field of 512 B or more as its own NIC scatter-gather entry (zero-copy transmit), and a per-buffer reference count keeps that memory alive until the DMA completes. A per-field size threshold, checked when the field's smart pointer (CFBytes/CFPtr) is constructed, chooses copy or zero-copy: smaller fields go into an arena-backed copy buffer, because below about 512 B the reference-count cache miss costs more than the memcpy. Serialize-and-send writes the packet header, the object header and the copied data into one entry and posts the zero-copy entries directly onto the NIC ring, with no intermediate scatter-gather array (a 7.7-17.4% throughput gain in the paper). All framing (a field bitmap plus u32 size/offset forward pointers) is at the front of the object, so each zero-copy field needs only one extra scatter-gather entry.
when_to_use: Microsecond-scale datacenter services such as caches and KV stores that already run on kernel bypass with Mellanox ConnectX-5/6 or Intel E810 NICs, where serialization copies are a large share of CPU time per request.

Responses built from values of 512 B or more that already sit in pinned memory, e.g. a store that returns stored blobs. On the paper's CDN image trace (objects of 1 KB and up) it served 97-128% more objects/s than the three baselines.

Workloads that mix small and large values, like the Twitter cache trace (about 32% of requests are 512 B or more), where the hybrid copy/zero-copy path beat pure scatter-gather by 2.3-3.9% and beat the copy-based libraries by 15.4-45.9%.
Applications that never modify data in place while it is being sent, such as Redis-style stores, versioned stores, or code that updates by allocating and swapping pointers.
As a reference design and threshold-calibration method (paper Section 5) when adding zero-copy serialization to your own kernel-bypass stack.
when_not_to_use: Small-field workloads. On Google's field-size distribution (94.9% of fields are 512 B or less) it ties or slightly trails Protobuf (844.7 vs 852.5 k req/s at 1 value) and wins only at 1-8 and 1-16 values per list.
Standard Linux sockets. The linux-datapath returns usize::MAX as its copy threshold (always copies), and many of its functions are unimplemented!().

Messages larger than one jumbo frame. The prototype has no segmentation: the CDN benchmark split objects into sub-objects that fit a jumbo frame, and the copy path carries a 'doesn't work if buffer is > than an MTU' TODO.

Production or multicore use, or any need for Protobuf wire compatibility, proto2 required fields, or recursive pointer-based types (the author confirms in issue #7 that trees with pointers are not supported). The paper evaluates a single-core server and leaves multicore to future work.
Any project that needs a license: the repo has no LICENSE file.

integration.dependencies: Cargo workspace crates (cornflakes-codegen, cornflakes-libos, cornflakes-utils, a datapath crate) used as path dependencies with build.rs code generation; git forks of bumpalo (and optionally demikernel); protobuf-parser, rdma-core and DPDK git submodules; Mellanox OFED 5.6-2.0.9.0 or Intel ice drivers (Intel also needs igb_uio binding); hugepages. protoc/flatc/capnp are needed only to build the baselines.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 2021 edition. install-rust.sh installs 1.70.0 and then switches the default to stable, so the rustc version is not pinned. Only Ubuntu 20.04 is tested.
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux (Ubuntu 20.04) with Mellanox ConnectX-5/ConnectX-6 (mlx5) or Intel E810 (ice) NICs; DPDK support is partial; the paper's runs use jumbo frames (MTU 9000)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The datapath creates one connection per thread from per-thread contexts. The paper's servers run on a single core, and multicore is left to future work. Nothing prevents the application from modifying a buffer that the NIC is still sending.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it reuses Protobuf's proto3 schema language and a Protobuf-like getter/setter API, but it has its own wire format, networking stack and pinned-buffer allocator, so neither application code nor wire data carry over unchanged

gotchas: The kv app's --copy_threshold CLI default and the mlx5 datapath default are both 256 B, not the paper's 512 B. The experiment configs pass 512 explicitly (cornflakes-dynamic-512). The paper recommends re-measuring the threshold on your own NIC and CPU.
Zero-copy applies only to data inside the stack's registered pinned memory. For any other pointer, recover_metadata returns None and the field is copied without any warning.
Copied entries come before zero-copy entries on the wire. As a result, peers configured with different thresholds can serialize repeated elements in different orders.
Issue #1, open since 2021: the code generator emits code with lifetime errors for messages that contain only int32 fields.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over rkyv, or over FlatBuffers-family formats such as Karmem and Lite³, only when your bottleneck is the transmit-path memcpy on a kernel-bypass NIC and your fields are 512 B or larger. Those siblings speed up CPU encode/decode over any transport, but Cornflakes's gain comes from NIC scatter-gather and disappears for small fields or on normal sockets.
verified_claims_summary: The SOSP 2023 paper runs a single-core Rust KV server on CloudLab c6525-100g machines (2x EPYC 7402P, ConnectX-5Ex 100 Gb, MTU 9000), with every system on the Cornflakes UDP stack and the pure-Rust protobuf 3.0.3, flatbuffers 2.1.2 and capnp 0.13.6 crates as baselines; the rustc version is not stated. Cornflakes served 366.5k vs 161.0-186.1k objects/s on the CDN image trace, delivered 15.4-45.9% more throughput on the Twitter trace (p99 about 52-61 us) and roughly tied on Google's small-field trace; in Redis, get/mget/lrange gained 15-40.1% over Redis's own handwritten serialization.
status_note: Abandoned research prototype: the main branch was last committed on 2023-07-27 (the timetrace branch on 2024-01-19), and there is no LICENSE file, so use it as a reference design to study, not as a dependency.
